## Newton's Method

We considered another approach with Newton's method[^newtons-method-1], which finds the roots of a function $f(x)$. In this case, we can find the decimal value of $x^*=\frac{1}{d}$ so that $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}-x^*=0.$ Think of $x^*$ as an unknown decimal that we're looking for.

[^newtons-method-1]: **Newton's method** available from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_method

We use Newton's formula $f(x^*)\approx f(x_n)+f'(x_n)(x^*-x_n)$, and set $f(x^*)=0:$ $$x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$$

$$x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}=x_n-\frac{\frac{1}{x_n}-d}{\frac{-1}{x_n^2}}=x_n+x_n^2(\frac{1}{x_n}-d)=x_n+(x_n-x_n^2d)$$

$$x_{n+1}=2x_n-x_n^2d$$

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="**Remark**"}
See an independently developed discussion in Prantl et al.[^newtons-method-2]
:::

[^newtons-method-2]: Prantl et al.; **Quo Vadis CKKS: Comparison of the realization of basic mathematical functions for the homomorphic cryptosystem CKKS using De Bello and polynomial approximations** available from https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214212625001474#sec2

This allows us to approximate $1/x$ in a chain of $2n$ multiplications and $n$ additions. We can do a simple test of approximating $\frac{1}{48}$ with Newton's method versus a geometric series as follows:

@fig-newton-digits measures accuracy by the number of correct decimal digits, defined as $-\log_{10}|\text{error}|$: an error of $10^{-4}$ is 4 correct digits. Both methods start from $x_0 = 1/64$ and are plotted after each iteration.

```{r}
#| label: fig-newton-digits
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| dev.args: !expr list(bg = "transparent")
#| fig-cap: "Correct decimal digits, $-\\log_{10}|x_n - 1/48|$, after each iteration for Newton's method and a scaled geometric series approximating $1/48$, both started from $x_0 = 1/64$ (plaintext)."
#| fig-alt: "A line plot of correct decimal digits against integer iteration count from 0 to 13. Both lines start at about 2.3 digits at iteration 0. The orange dashed Newton line climbs steeply to about 11.3 digits at iteration 4, crossing the 10 digit line there. The blue dot-dash geometric series line rises steadily and reaches 10 digits at iteration 13."

library(ggplot2)

neutral <- "grey50"
book_theme <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.15),
      axis.title = element_text(color = "grey50"),
      axis.text = element_text(color = "grey50")
    )
}

d <- 48
x0 <- 1 / 64          # same start for both methods
target <- 1 / d
k <- 0:13

# Newton: x_{n+1} = 2 x_n - d x_n^2
newton <- numeric(5)
newton[1] <- x0
for (i in 2:5) newton[i] <- 2 * newton[i - 1] - d * newton[i - 1]^2

# Scaled geometric series: S_n = x0 * sum_{j=0}^{n} (1 - d x0)^j, r = 1/4
r <- 1 - d * x0
geo <- x0 * cumsum(r^k)

# Correct decimal digits = -log10 |error| (not rounded, so the doubling is visible)
digits <- function(v) -log10(abs(v - target))
digit_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(iter = 0:4, digits = digits(newton), method = "Newton"),
  data.frame(iter = k, digits = digits(geo), method = "Geometric series")
)

digit_data$method <- factor(digit_data$method, levels = c("Newton", "Geometric series"))
cols <- c(Newton = "#E69F00", `Geometric series` = "#56B4E9")
ltys <- c(Newton = "dashed", `Geometric series` = "dotdash")

ggplot(digit_data, aes(iter, digits, color = method, linetype = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, color = neutral, linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 13, y = 10.7, label = "10 correct digits", color = neutral,
           size = 5, hjust = 1) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.4, y = 11.2, label = "Newton", color = cols[["Newton"]],
           size = 5, fontface = "bold", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 8.2, y = 4.4, label = "Geometric series",
           color = cols[["Geometric series"]], size = 5, fontface = "bold", hjust = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cols) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = ltys) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:13) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 12, 2), limits = c(0, 12)) +
  guides(color = "none", linetype = "none") +
  labs(x = "Iteration (integer count)", y = "Correct decimal digits, -log10|error|") +
  book_theme()
```


The one catch with Newton's method is that in order to be effective, it has to initially guess reasonably close to the root.

### Guessing a Starting Point

Naively, one (impossible) approach would be to make some different buckets of $n$ based on powers of $2$:

|    n     | $ct_{2^n}$ | $ct_{2^{-n}}$ |
|:--------:|:----------:|:-------------:|
|    0     |     1      |       1       |
|    1     |     2      | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
|    2     |     4      | $\frac{1}{4}$ |
| $\vdots$ |  $\vdots$  |   $\vdots$    |
|    33    |  $2^{33}$  |   $2^{-33}$   |

Note: we only go to $n=33$ since $\log_2(10^{10})\approx33$, where $10^{-10}$ is the approximate "round to zero" threshold. This would need a tweak to include negatives.

What we want to do is to figure out where the divisor belongs based on where $n$ belongs, and then make our guess $x_0$ be based on the corresponding boundary bucket. Sadly, this does not work because we cannot (yet) do different executions depending on branching logic.

Unless we try some more complex methods, we will need to come up with a universal $x_0$ guess[^newtons-method-3] that will work regardless of what $\frac{1}{x}$ is.

[^newtons-method-3]: Prantl et al.; **De Bello Homomorphico: Investigation of the extensibility of the OpenFHE library with basic mathematical functions by means of common approaches using the example of the CKKS cryptosystem** available from https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10207-023-00781-0

Fortunately, the basin of convergence[^newtons-method-4] for Newton's method approximation of $\frac{1}{x}$ is $\big(0,\frac{2}{x}\big)$ if $x>0$ and $\big(\frac{2}{x},0\big)$ if $x<0$.

[^newtons-method-4]: Knott et al.; **CRYPTEN: Secure Multi-Party Computation Meets Machine Learning** available from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2109.00984

1.  To guarantee convergence we can simply pick the closest number to zero that does not get eliminated by rounding, maybe $\approx 10^{-10}$ or $-(10^{-10})$, depending on the sign of $\frac{1}{x}$ (which needs to be known), every time.
2.  If we want to account for the sign and have a Sign function, we would be able to capture it with something like $(x<0)*(x_0=-(10^{-10}))+(x>0)*(x_0=10^{-10})$. See Section IV for similar methods.

@fig-newton-cobweb shows the iteration $g(x) = 2x - dx^2$ for $d = 11$ as a staircase between the curve and the line $y = x$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-newton-cobweb
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| dev.args: !expr list(bg = "transparent")
#| fig-cap: "Cobweb diagram of the Newton iteration $x_{n+1} = g(x_n) = 2x_n - dx_n^2$ for $d = 11$ (plaintext), started at $x_0 = 0.01$. The iterates climb to the fixed point $1/d = 1/11$, where the parabola peaks and crosses $y = x$."
#| fig-alt: "A plot of the parabola g of x equals 2x minus 11 x squared as a solid grey curve and the line y equals x as a dashed grey line. An orange staircase starts at x equals 0.01 on the horizontal axis, steps up to the parabola and across to the line, and climbs toward the point where the curves meet at x equal to 1 over 11, about 0.0909. The steps shrink as they approach that fixed point, which sits at the top of the parabola."

library(ggplot2)

neutral <- "grey50"
book_theme <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.15),
      axis.title = element_text(color = "grey50"),
      axis.text = element_text(color = "grey50")
    )
}

d <- 11
g <- function(x) 2 * x - d * x^2
fixed <- 1 / d

# Iterate x_{n+1} = g(x_n) from x0 = 0.01 and build the cobweb path:
# up to the curve, then across to the line y = x, repeatedly.
steps <- 6
x <- numeric(steps + 1)
x[1] <- 0.01
for (i in 1:steps) x[i + 1] <- g(x[i])
path <- data.frame(x = x[1], y = 0)
for (i in 1:steps) {
  path <- rbind(path, data.frame(x = c(x[i], x[i + 1]), y = c(x[i + 1], x[i + 1])))
}
iterates <- data.frame(x = x[1:5], label = paste0("x[", 0:4, "]"))

curve_data <- data.frame(x = seq(0, 2 * fixed, length.out = 300))
curve_data$y <- g(curve_data$x)

ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = neutral, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = curve_data, aes(x, y), color = neutral, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(data = curve_data, aes(x, x), color = neutral, linewidth = 0.9,
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_path(data = path, aes(x, y), color = "#E69F00", linewidth = 0.9,
            arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "inches"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(x = fixed, y = fixed), aes(x, y), size = 3,
             color = "#E69F00") +
  annotate("text", x = fixed - 0.004, y = fixed + 0.008, label = "fixed~point~1/d",
           parse = TRUE, color = "#E69F00", size = 5, fontface = "bold", hjust = 1) +
  geom_text(data = iterates[1:3, ], aes(x = x, y = -0.006, label = label),
            parse = TRUE, color = "#E69F00", size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.155, y = 0.065, label = "y == g(x)", parse = TRUE,
           color = neutral, size = 5, fontface = "bold", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.12, y = 0.165, label = "y == x", parse = TRUE,
           color = neutral, size = 5, fontface = "bold", hjust = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2 * fixed), ylim = c(-0.008, 0.19), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "g(x)") +
  book_theme()
```

3.  If we have additional knowledge about the actual range of values, e.g. if we know that values are in $[a,b]$ then we can uuse something like the geometric mean $1/\sqrt{ab}$. (concretely, if weight is always between $50$ and $5000$ pounds, we can take an initial guess of 1/500).

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="**Disclaimers**"}
1.  The "closest number to $0$" method might cause overflow issues. This would require testing.
2.  Starting so close to zero makes a very steep derivative of $\frac{1}{x}$ at that point, leading to the second guess $x_1$ being within the error bound of $x_0$: a sort of false convergence. Even attempting a remedy with stricter difference criteria leads to 30+ iterations before true convergence, wiping out some of the initial savings, which in fact may be more expensive than the geometric series.
:::
